intro_facts.claim: The 'Zacher Epitome' (Iulii Valerii epitome) is an anonymous Latin abridgement of Julius Valerius' Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis, the Latin version of Ps.-Callisthenes, recension α. It is named after its first and only editor, Julius Zacher (Halle 1867). The manuscript headings vary: 'Exceptio historiae Magni Alexandri Regis Macedonum' (H), 'Incipit vita Alexandri Regis magni Macedonis' (B), 'Incipit textus de ortu Magni Alexandri Macedonis' (E). Zacher notes that none of his manuscripts calls the text an epitome, and Siemoneit (n. 3) says the same.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, pp. III–VII (preface, archive.org juliivaleriiepi00zachgoog); Siemoneit 2023, p. 199 n. 3

intro_facts.claim: The date is only a terminus ante quem. The oldest manuscripts date from the early 9th century: Den Haag, KB 74 J 9 and Leiden, Voss. lat. Q 20 (s. IX¹; Jakobi adds 'aus Tours'). Voss. lat. Q 20 is also the oldest Curtius manuscript and is dated to the first quarter of the 9th century. Jakobi says the usual dating to the 8th–9th century is not secure and the Epitome could be considerably older. Zacher (1867, p. IV) already argued that it predates the 9th century, because 9th-century copies show errors typical of copying from older exemplars that were hard to read. Siemoneit (p. 199 n. 3) says the oldest known manuscript is from the early 9th century and treats that as a terminus ante quem.
intro_facts.source: Jakobi 2019, RhM 162, p. 84 n. 4, p. 85 n. 5, p. 92 n. 21; Zacher 1867, p. IV; Siemoneit 2023, p. 199 n. 3

intro_facts.claim: Zacher's H (The Hague, 'königliche Bibliothek no. 830', s. IX, 'wahrscheinlich in Italien geschrieben') is probably the manuscript that Jakobi cites as Den Haag KB 74 J 9. Zacher used only one Hague manuscript, but I have not checked the concordance of the two shelfmarks.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, p. V; Jakobi 2019, p. 84 n. 4

intro_facts.claim: Origin is disputed. Rosellini proposes an Italian origin, and Jakobi, following M. D. Reeve (RFIC 123, 1997, 371), doubts it.
intro_facts.source: Jakobi 2019, p. 84 n. 4 (Reeve not seen directly)

intro_facts.claim: Number of manuscripts: Ross (1956) lists 68 manuscripts of the Epitome, against three nearly complete manuscripts of the full Julius Valerius. Voorbij (1984, p. 117) writes: 'At the present time 80 Epitome manuscripts are known.' Jakobi 2019 and Siemoneit 2023 both give 80, citing Ross and Voorbij. The figure of 67 on Wikipedia does not match either list.
intro_facts.source: Ross, Scriptorium 10 (1956) 127 (Persée page images); Voorbij, Scriptorium 38 (1984) 117; Jakobi 2019, p. 84 n. 4; Siemoneit 2023, p. 199 n. 2

intro_facts.claim:
Zacher's sources. He copied or collated six manuscripts himself:
- H: The Hague 830, s. IX.
- L: Leiden, Voss. lat. Q 20, s. IX.
- A: Leiden, Voss. lat. Q 29, s. X.
- B: Leiden, BPL 20, s. XII, from Bec; a learned scribe who often 'improved' the text.
- D: Wolfenbüttel 'Ms. Aug. 7.4.4', probably s. XII; arbitrarily rewritten, with the Epistola ad Aristotelem inserted into the narrative. Voorbij lists Wolfenbüttel 2963 (7.4 Aug. 4°) among the interpolated Epitome texts.
- E: Wolfenbüttel 'Ms. Aug. 56.16.8', s. X; Zacher's best manuscript.
To these he added C, Perizonius' copy (Leiden, Periz. Q 9) of Oxford, Corpus Christi College 82 (s. XII), which breaks off in ch. 5. Voorbij and Jakobi count these as the 'seven' manuscripts. Other material:
- Paris BN lat. 8518 (s. X–XI) and 8519 (s. XIII), only for 1,1–7, through Berger de Xivrey's printed excerpts.
- Two unidentified Vatican manuscripts, through Mai's supplements.
- Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Venice 1494), for a few passages.
- The full Julius Valerius: the Turin palimpsest, the Ambrosianus and Paris lat. 4880.
- The Greek manuscripts A, B, C and Leiden Vulc. 93.
Zacher assembled text and apparatus in haste for the Halle philologists' meeting (dedication dated 1 Oct. 1867, preface 9 Sept. 1867) and emended only rarely.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, pp. V–XIV; Voorbij 1984, p. 117 and n. 9; Jakobi 2019, p. 84 n. 4

intro_facts.claim: Numbering. Zacher gave the continuous text the book and chapter division of C. Müller's edition of Ps.-Callisthenes and Julius Valerius (Paris, Didot 1846), adding Mai's numbers in brackets. He states that Book I excerpts chapters 1–15, 17–26, 29, 30, 34–42, 46 and 47, which is exactly the set in our book1.json; everything else is omitted. Kübler (1888) numbers Book I in 54 chapters following Mai's second edition and prints Müller's Roman numerals in the margin, so Kübler's chapter numbers differ from Zacher's.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, p. XII; Kübler 1888, conspectus siglorum before p. 1 and margins of pp. 1–65

intro_facts.claim: Rosellini's chapter numbers for Julius Valerius (Teubner 1993; ed. corr. 2004) coincide with Müller's and therefore with Zacher's. The evidence is that Siemoneit and Jakobi cite, for example, Iul. Val. 1,24,690 (Pausanias), 1,26,770–773 (army funds), 1,30,800–814 (Ammon) and 1,46,1568 (Thebes), and these equal Zacher's chapter numbers. I have not seen Rosellini's edition itself.
intro_facts.source: Jakobi 2019 (Siemoneit 2023 does not cite Iul. Val. 1,24,690 or 1,46,1568); Jakobi 2019, pp. 86–89

intro_facts.claim: Ps.-Callisthenes α in Kroll 1926 uses the same chapter numbers as Müller in Book I. I spot-checked Kroll's chapter markers at 1.14, 1.38, 1.40, 1.41, 1.43, 1.46, 1.46a (Ismenias) and 1.47 (Clitomachus). Kroll states that chapters 27–28 occur only in recension β ('Hinc deflectit B′ solus tradens c. 27 sq.'). Julius Valerius also lacks them: Kübler's margin jumps from XXVI to XXIX.
intro_facts.source: Kroll 1926, pp. 26 app., 45–62 (archive.org historiaalexandr00pseu); Kübler 1888, pp. 30–31

intro_facts.claim: Book I of the Epitome does not end with Alexander's accession. It runs on to the Italian, Libyan and Egyptian campaigns, Tyre, the exchange of letters with Darius and the first victory, the destruction of Thebes, and Clitomachus at the Isthmian games at Corinth (ch. 47).

The epitomator keeps the opening fairly fully and cuts more and more as the text goes on. In Book III he omits or barely mentions the Brahmans, the Amazons and the letters to Aristotle and Olympias. He tries to keep Valerius' own wording, which sometimes produces odd sentences. Overall the text is reduced to about one third.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, pp. XII–XIII; Siemoneit 2023, p. 214 ('auf rund ein Drittel reduziert')

intro_facts.claim: The Epitome has textual value for Julius Valerius. Jakobi calls it the only complete witness to the text. Only Z and its descendant O, the Oxford epitome, preserve the opening chapters. Kübler printed Book I ch. 1 and the beginning of ch. 2 (= Zacher chs. 1–3 and the first sentence of 4) from Zacher's Epitome. An early second hand in the Ambrosianus entered readings from Z (Rosellini p. XXI, per Jakobi).
intro_facts.source: Jakobi 2019, pp. 85, 87 n. 11, 89 n. 14; Kübler 1888, note before p. 1 ('Libri primi caput primum et initium capitis secundi supplevi ex Epitoma a Zachero edita')

intro_facts.claim: The Oxford and Montpellier epitomes. Oxford, Corpus Christi College 82 (s. XII) is Kübler's siglum O and the subject of Cillié's dissertation (De Iulii Valerii epitoma Oxoniensi, Strassburg 1905). It is a later, expanded form of Z: the Epitome is enlarged with clauses and whole sections taken from the full Julius Valerius, partly undoing Z's cuts. Montpellier H 31 (s. XIII) is described by Ross as an Epitome 'expanded with additions from the complete text of Julius Valerius'. Voorbij calls the two together the 'Oxford-Montpellier Epitome', an interpolated version edited by A. Hilka in Romanische Forschungen 29 (1911); Voorbij gives pp. 31–69, Jakobi pp. 34–69. Siemoneit says Montpellier differs only slightly from Oxford. Romano's thesis that O was Z's model and dates from the 4th–5th century is refuted on stemmatic grounds, since O shares Z's errors. Another interpolated version is the Liegnitz 'Historia Alexandri Magni' (15th c.; Hilka 1911, pp. 1–30), and Zacher's D is a further interpolated witness.
intro_facts.source: Ross 1956, p. 128 n. 12–13, p. 130; Voorbij 1984, p. 117 n. 9; Jakobi 2019, p. 85 and n. 6; Siemoneit 2023, p. 199 nn. 5–6; Kübler 1888, conspectus siglorum

intro_facts.claim: Medieval reception, Latin. Zacher states that Vincent of Beauvais took most of the Epitome into the Speculum historiale. In his view, though, its influence on Western Alexander literature was subordinate and partly indirect; the Historia de preliis was the main basis. Ross (1956) calls the Epitome one of the most important sources of medieval Alexander romances and chronicles. Voorbij studied it as a source of Helinand of Froidmont's Chronicon and Vincent's Speculum historiale. Buntz (1973), cited by Siemoneit, calls it the most popular and widespread version of the Alexander story until the 12th century.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, p. IV; Ross 1956, p. 127; Voorbij 1984, p. 117; Siemoneit 2023, p. 199 n. 4 (Buntz not seen)

intro_facts.claim: Alberic of Pisançon/Besançon (early 12th c.), and through him Lamprecht's Alexanderlied (c. 1150s), drew on Julius Valerius, either the full text or the Epitome. Kinzel (1884) found it hard to decide which. Lamprecht agrees with the full Julius Valerius against the Epitome in some places, for example Alexander's threat about the Persian tribute and 'paucis admodum comitatus'. In others he agrees with the Epitome, notably Darius' threat to have Alexander beaten (Epit. 1,36 'verberibus affectum' ~ Lamprecht v. 1486). Ross (1963, p. 9), cited via Wikipedia, says Alberic used both Julius Valerius and the Zacher Epitome.
intro_facts.source: Kinzel 1884, pp. XLVI–XLVII (archive.org lamprechtsalexan00lampuoft); Wikipedia 'Alberic of Besançon' citing Ross, Alexander Historiatus (1963) 9–10

intro_facts.claim: Thomas of Kent's Anglo-Norman Roman de toute chevalerie derives mainly from the Zacher Epitome. Wikipedia, citing van Melle & Gerritsen (2000), also lists the Roman d'Alexandre and the Histoire ancienne jusqu'à César among works it influenced. I have not checked these against Cary or the ANTS edition.
intro_facts.source: Wikipedia 'Thomas de Kent' citing Cary, The Medieval Alexander (1956) 35–36; Wikipedia 'Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis' citing van Melle & Gerritsen 2000, p. 21

intro_facts.claim: Main recent study: G. Siemoneit, 'Die Zacher-Epitome. Änderungen, Erweiterungen, Auslassungen', in H. Wulfram (ed.), Der lateinische ›Alexanderroman‹ des Iulius Valerius: Sprache, Erzählung, Kontext (Millennium-Studien 101), Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter 2023. Crossref gives pp. 199–220 (not 199–219). DOI 10.1515/9783111091679-012; open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. The author is affiliated with Paderborn/Bielefeld.
intro_facts.source: Crossref API for ISBN 9783111091679; Unpaywall; official PDF, De Gruyter 2023 (text pp. 199–219, p. 220 blank)

intro_facts.claim: Julius Valerius' translation predates c. 340, because the Itinerarium Alexandri uses its wording (Zacher). The Wulfram volume dates it to the early 4th century CE.
intro_facts.source: Zacher 1867, p. III; Wulfram 2023 publisher blurb

intro_facts.claim: Translation status: I found no complete translation of the Zacher Epitome into any modern language. There is one caveat. Translations of the full Julius Valerius, such as J.-P. Callu's bilingual French edition (Turnhout 2010) or G. Berengo's Italian translation of Mai's text (Venice 1851/52), may render the opening chapters (Zacher 1–3), which editors take from the Epitome. I have not checked whether they do.
intro_facts.source: Web searches (EN/DE/IT/RU); Jakobi 2019, p. 92 n. 19 (Callu 2010); bookseller and article notices of Berengo

siemoneit_book1:
SOURCE. Checked against the official open-access PDF (De Gruyter 2023, DOI 10.1515/9783111091679-012, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); page numbers are the printed ones (text pp. 199–219, p. 220 blank). Two independent readings: raw/siemoneit-check.json. Every Book I example below was also checked against Kübler's Latin. (An earlier version of this summary was made from an unauthorised mirror; it has been replaced.)

WHAT SIEMONEIT SAYS
1. (pp. 199–200, nn. 2–7.) The Epitome (Z), made 'im 9. Jahrhundert oder davor' (the oldest manuscript, early 9th c., is a terminus ante quem: n. 3, after Jakobi 2019, 85), is the oldest member of a family of epitomes of the Res gestae and 'nahezu vollständig' displaced the original; 80 manuscripts (n. 2, citing Voorbij and Ross — but Ross 1956 has 68). Until the 12th c. it was 'die beliebteste und am meisten verbreitete Version des Alexanderstoffes' (Buntz 1973, 11; n. 4). The later Oxford epitome partly undoes Z's cuts (n. 5); Montpellier differs only slightly from Oxford. The Metz epitome ('wohl' 4th/5th c.) and the Liegnitz epitome (a 15th-c. reworking of the Res gestae) lie outside this family (n. 6; but n. 59 on p. 216 is inconsistent about Liegnitz). Author, aims and date are unknown, and the text has been little studied (p. 200).
2. Method (pp. 200–209). A genre-theoretical discussion of epitomising (pp. 200–204; Galen's Synopsis de pulsibus p. 202, Genette's minimal story p. 203 n. 27). Collation of Z with Rosellini's 2004 text using CollateX (p. 205 n. 35; the TEI of Z is cited there). Fig. 1 (p. 209) plots each chapter's length in characters as a percentage of Valerius'; word- and sentence-level cosine and Ratcliff/Obershelp similarity give comparable values (p. 208 n. 46). The regression line shows the cuts growing through the work, Book III least like its source. Overall Z is about one third of the original (pp. 208, 214).
3. Changes and expansions (pp. 205–208). Minimal and sense-preserving, but 'nicht konsequent durchgehalten' (p. 208):
- word order (p. 206): 1,4 'promit tabulas', 'huius peritiae'; 1,12 'totius mundi'; 1,13 'nutrix eius';
- historic presents replaced by past tenses (p. 206);
- commoner expressions (pp. 206–207): 1,36 'latronum' for 'latrocinantium'; 1,18 'quintum decimum agens annum' for 'quintum et decimum ingressus annum'; 1,7 'mane facto' (Z p. 9 l. 8) for 'mane lucescente' (Iul. Val. 1,7,150), the latter rare, the former 'ab der Spätantike immerhin rund 500 Belege' (p. 207);
- small clarifying expansions: 1,36 'quo tibi tuisque necessaria emas' (p. 207);
- rare words kept: 'beluile' (1,13) and 'lusitatio' (1,36) (p. 208); small-word substitutions listed in n. 45.
4. Omissions (pp. 208–214). Only 1,2 and 1,36 pass into Z more or less unchanged; whole chapters, speeches, oracle and dream episodes are dropped (p. 208). Showing turned into telling (p. 209): 1,6, Olympias' dream report becomes 'eique somnii retulit visionem' — nothing is lost, the prophecy was given in 1,4 (pp. 209–210); 1,26, the sum of 14,460 talents and the second source of funds give way to 'abundantissime' (p. 210). Mai in 1835 suppressed Z from the end of 1,5 to 1,10 as indecent (p. 209 n. 47). Three heuristic themes:
(a) Historiography (pp. 210–211): battle details 'regelmäßig erspart' — the battle against Darius (Iul. Val. 1,41,1361–1373) reduced to the cum-clause 'cum ergo diu spes exitus fluctuaret…' (n. 50; Siemoneit cites 'Z 1,42 p. 34 l. 6–7', but the clause is in ch. 41); speeches cut, e.g. Demosthenes, 2,3–4 (p. 211).
(b) The image of Alexander (pp. 211–213): he cuts 'bevorzugt' where a passage shows a flaw or misconduct. 1,13: Valerius says the child resembled neither Philip, nor his mother, nor the man from whose seed he was believed to come; Z keeps only 'Erat autem vultu et forma pulcherrimus' (pp. 211–212). 2,15: Alexander's small stature disappears (p. 212). 1,46: Alexander's demand for 1,000 Theban soldiers, the Thebans' refusal and 'violentia Alexandri' are omitted, so the attack is even less motivated (pp. 212–213).
(c) Pagan mythology (pp. 213–214; anticipated by Stoneman 1999, n. 53): gods, sacrifices and oracle interpretations become rare; Ammon is named 'genau dreimal' (1,4; 1,7; 1,10) — in fact also in 1,8 ('deus est Libyae, Ammon nomine') and 3,18 — and never as Alexander's father; the 1,30 Libya/Ammon episode shrinks to 'Hinc igitur pergens omnem Libyam peragrat' (also p. 203 n. 24); in 2,13 the dream motive for the envoy disguise is gone (p. 214).
5. Conclusion (pp. 214–217). The redactor 'wahrscheinlich' knew Latin well; edits 'weitgehend systematisch und konsequent' (p. 214; contrast p. 208). A 'Harmlos-Fassung' of the Res gestae, 'gewissermaßen' (p. 214): simpler vocabulary, syntax closer to Vulgar Latin, about one third of the length; a skeleton of the main episodes, especially in Books 2–3, probably meant to replace the original (p. 215). ARI 16.58 against 21.45 (pp. 214–215, nn. 54–58; Fig. 2 p. 216). Alexander appears as 'strahlender Held'; a pro-Christian context is likely, possibly use in world chronicles or Bible-related settings (p. 216, n. 59). The date cannot be narrowed; Leo of Naples (10th c.) kept pagan mythology and battles, and whether this argues for an earlier date of Z is left open (p. 216, n. 60). He calls the author 'unser spätantiker oder frühmittelalterlicher Epitomator' (p. 217).
6. Open question for Book I (pp. 216–217). Why did the epitomator shorten the beginning of Book I 'vergleichsweise wenig' and keep 'die fabulöse Nectanabus-Episode'? Two guesses, both as questions: sensationalism, since the Alexander historians do not know it, or loss of interest as the work went on.

MY OWN COLLATION OF BOOK I AGAINST KÜBLER, ADDING TO SIEMONEIT (none of this is in his chapter)
- Lysias' wedding jibe, which implies that Alexander is illegitimate, is replaced by a vague invented sentence (1,21).
- In the Pausanias story (1,24), Valerius' 'ecquid mulier consentiret … neque id ei ex sententia provenisset' becomes 'et mulier consentiret', with the failure clause missing, so Olympias seems to consent. A similar corruption is in the Ambrosianus (Kübler's apparatus; Calderan, Rosellini and Jakobi).
- 'Ab Ammone dicta' becomes 'deum … praedixisse' (1,24).
- The letters lose Darius' title 'consessor dei Mithrae' and Alexander's 'filius Ammonis' (1,35–38).
- Additions: 'quondam conscolasticus eius' for Nicolaus (1,18), absent from the Julius Valerius manuscripts; 'Atque his dictis roborat pavitantia corda suorum' (1,37); Darius as 'praecursor' of the flight (1,41); Alexander called 'tyranni' in 1,46.
translation_status:
Status: no modern translation of the Zacher Epitome found in Russian, English, German, French, Italian or Spanish.

Searches run: English, German, Italian and Russian web searches on 'Zacher Epitome / Iulii Valerii epitome / Epitome des Iulius Valerius / epitome di Giulio Valerio / Эпитома Юлия Валерия' with 'translation / Übersetzung / traduzione / перевод'. I also checked the literature I read: Siemoneit 2023, Jakobi 2019, Voorbij 1984 and Ross 1956. None mentions a translation.

Coverage gaps: French and Spanish were covered only indirectly. I did not search WorldCat, SBN, BnF or RSL catalogues.

Caveats:
1. Translations of the full Julius Valerius may include the Epitome text for the opening chapters (Zacher chs. 1–3 and the start of 4). Editors take those chapters from the Epitome because the Julius Valerius manuscripts lack them (Kübler 1888, note before p. 1; Jakobi 2019, p. 85). Candidates are J.-P. Callu's bilingual 'Julius Valère, Roman d'Alexandre' (Turnhout 2010, cited by Jakobi) and G. Berengo's Italian translation of Mai's Julius Valerius (Venice 1851/52), whose Mai text had gaps filled from the Epitome. I have not checked either.
2. Hilka's editions of the interpolated Oxford-Montpellier and Liegnitz versions are Latin editions, not translations.

Conclusion: a translation of the Epitome as such appears to be a first, but the claim should be worded as 'as far as we could establish'.

parallels.jv: No independent Julius Valerius text. Kübler 1888 cap. 1 (p. 1) prints the Epitome's own text here (Müller I), and per Jakobi only Z and O preserve the opening.
parallels.change: Compared with the Greek only, since Valerius is lost here, so I cannot tell whether Valerius or the epitomator made these changes. The Latin keeps 'descended from gods', measuring the earth and counting the stars, but drops the taming of the sea and measuring the Nile, and the note that Nectanebo was Egypt's last king. The bowl holds spring water instead of rainwater (as in the Armenian and β). Nectanebo invokes 'deos superos inferosque' instead of angels and the Libyan god Ammon. The wax figures come alive (as in the Armenian and β).

parallels.jv: No independent Julius Valerius text. Kübler cap. 1, p. 1 (from the Epitome; Müller II).
parallels.ps_call_alpha: Ps.-Call. α 1.2 (Kroll p. 2); chapter boundary per Müller, not separately checked in Kroll
parallels.change: The Greek scene of a commander reporting the invasion, and Nectanebo's speech that strength lies in courage, not numbers, is reduced to a bare report and his laughter. The list of nations differs: Kroll's apparatus notes that 'Val.' adds Phoenices, Parthi and Assyrii (Indi also appear in the Armenian), and the Bosporans, Chaldaeans and others are missing.

parallels.jv: No independent Julius Valerius text. Kübler cap. 2 (p. 2) prints the Epitome; the Turin palimpsest starts only at 'longe celebratior' in ch. 4 (Müller III).
parallels.change: In the Greek, Nectanebo sees the gods of Egypt steering the enemy ships; the Latin has only 'quibus intellexit se vincendum'. The route via Pelusium and the arrival at Pella are absent. The Egyptians' oracle (the king will return young) is lacking here; Kroll notes 'om. Val.', and in Valerius it appears later with the statue in 1,34. He shaves his head, wears linen and poses as an astrologer, as in the Greek.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,4 (Rosellini/Müller IV) = Kübler cap. 2–3, pp. 2–4 (Turin palimpsest T from 'longe celebratior')
parallels.change: Reordering: the greeting without 'domina' comes before the falling in love. Dropped: Valerius' remark on Nectanebo's lustfulness; Olympias' praise of his truthfulness; the ekphrasis of the pinax as a masterpiece; her sending the servants away; the exchange of birth charts, including Nectanebo's self-serving check whether his own chart matches hers; Olympias' question 'quanam id facultate?'; and the description of Ammon (young, grey-haired, ram-horned). Word order is normalised ('promit tabulas', 'huius peritiae', per Siemoneit). The list of planet-stones is kept.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,5 (Müller V) = Kübler cap. 4, p. 4
parallels.change: Almost verbatim. Dropped: 'neque oppertus in tempus longum', 'ex scientia', and the clause naming Ammon ('quos fore cum Ammone dixerat').

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,6 (Müller VI) = Kübler cap. 4, pp. 4–5 (Siemoneit: Iul. Val. 1,6,115–117)
parallels.change: Olympias' report of the dream, in direct speech in Valerius, becomes indirect ('eique somnii retulit visionem'). Her promise of fatherly regard for Nectanebo is dropped. His instructions are shortened: the lamps left burning, the veiled face and the sidelong look are gone. The serpent 'clementius reptabundus' becomes simply 'reptabundus'.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,7 (Müller VII) = Kübler cap. 4, pp. 5–7 (Siemoneit 1,7,150; Jakobi 1,7,153)
parallels.change: The disguise (ram's fleece with horns, sceptre, white robe) is kept. 'Mane iam luciscente' becomes 'mane facto'. The god's words are cut ('invicta et insubiugabilia foedera'), and 'sese' is normalised to 'se'. Dropped: Olympias' line about her love; Nectanebo's joy; the 'purgatione sacricula' rite; 'sub opinione Ammonis dei'; the narrator's comment on her being led by magic; and the promise that Ammon will instruct Philip in a dream.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,8 (Müller VIII) = Kübler cap. 4, pp. 7–8
parallels.change: The hawk's flight 'per terras et mare' is omitted, and 'iussis mandatis' picks up Valerius' 'ut iussum est' (Jakobi). Philip's dream is kept nearly verbatim. In the interpreters' speech, 'Consignatio enim fides…', 'vel carta' and 'in quo etiam deorum effigies veneramur' are cut. The final clause on Philip suspecting a human father is omitted. Z has plural 'interpretes', with T and P.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,9 (Müller IX) = Kübler cap. 4, p. 8
parallels.change: Olympias' fear and Nectanebo's comforting are dropped. Philip's speech is reduced to its opening and its last sentence; the pardon and the maxim that kings have no power over gods are gone. Olympias' thanks to Nectanebo are omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,10 (Müller X) = Kübler cap. 4, pp. 8–10 (Siemoneit: 1,10,232–241)
parallels.change: The banquet description, the serpent's forked-tongue kiss and Philip's frightened withdrawal are cut. 'Sobrius' becomes 'exhilaratus'. 'Sed auctiorem' is Zacher's correction, made against the Greek, and agrees with T. Ammon as 'Libyae dominum universae' is kept.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,11 (Müller XI) = Kübler cap. 5, pp. 10–11
parallels.change: 'In quadam regiae parte' becomes 'in quadam regione'. Philip's unease is dropped, as are Antiphon's divine inspiration ('dei adminiculo inspiratus') and the recap of the omen. The prophecy is paraphrased, and 'liquet' is added.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,12 (Müller XII) = Kübler cap. 6, p. 11 (Siemoneit 1,12,296)
parallels.change: Nectanebo's secretly touching Olympias and the astronomical detail are omitted; the cosmos at the summit of its turning and the sun at mid-heaven are gone. 'Mundi totius' becomes 'totius mundi'.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,13 (Müller XIII) = Kübler cap. 6 end–7, pp. 11–14 (Siemoneit 1,13,313–316, 323)
Iul. Val. 1,14 (Müller XIV) = Kübler cap. 7 end–8, pp. 14–16
parallels.change: Philip's speech to the twelve-year-old is omitted, and 'adpellens' becomes 'agens'. Added: 'nocte quadam' and 'nunc resupinus iacens'. Dropped: Nectanebo's 'laesum me letaliter sentio'; 'tractatum et amorem'; the boy's fear of leaving the body to beasts; Olympias' burial of Nectanebo with honour; and the closing reflection (Nectanebo, an Egyptian, buried in Macedonia; Alexander, a Macedonian, to be buried in Egypt).

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,15 (Müller XV) = Kübler cap. 9, p. 16
parallels.change: The Delphic oracle loses 'et hasta omnia subiugabit'. The etymology of Bucephalus (an ox-head brand on the haunch) and Philip's hope of a 'younger Heracles' are omitted. All of Müller XVI is skipped (Aristotle's question to the princes, the Zeuxis letters on spending), so there is no ch. 16.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,17 (Müller XVII) = Kübler cap. 9 end, pp. 19–20
parallels.change: Ptolemy's line is kept. The horse's gentle neigh and its gestures of submission are cut. 'Bucephala' becomes 'Bucephalus', and 'orbis integri dominum' becomes 'totius orbis dominum'.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,18 (Müller XVIII) = Kübler cap. 10–11, pp. 20–22 (Siemoneit 1,18,516; Jakobi 1,18,560)
parallels.change: The dialogue with Philip on which contest to enter is cut, and Hephaestion is omitted. Addition: Nicolaus is 'quondam conscolasticus eius'. This is in all Epitome manuscripts and in Vincent of Beauvais but absent from the Julius Valerius manuscripts (Zacher's apparatus: 'fehlt Vbc'). The exchange of insults is condensed, and the oath drops 'et Acernaniae telo'. 'Sputamenta' is shared with the Ambrosianus (Jakobi).

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,19 (Müller XIX) = Kübler cap. 12, pp. 22–23
parallels.change: Drastically reduced to one sentence. The nine named competitors, the race tactics, Nicolaus' crash and the Olympian priest's prophecy of world rule are all omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,20 (Müller XX) = Kübler cap. 13, pp. 23–24
parallels.change: Cleopatra's father ('Attali … filiae') and 'Gaudeo quidem quod in praesenti laetamini' are omitted, as is Philip's inner rage. 'Aliis regalibus nuptiis' (to another king) becomes 'iterum regalibus nuptiis'.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,21 (Müller XXI) = Kübler cap. 13, p. 24
parallels.change: Lysias' actual jibe, that Cleopatra will give Philip legitimate sons who look like him, implies that Alexander is a bastard. It is replaced by an invented neutral sentence about repeated jests and warnings. Alexander's taunt ('he who would cross Asia and Europe cannot cross a couch') and the Centaur/Lapith and Odysseus/suitors similes are omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,22 (Müller XXII) = Kübler cap. 14–15, pp. 24–26
parallels.change: Alexander's reproaches about Lysias and Philip's cruelty are trimmed, and so is his play on calling Philip 'father'. 'Iudex et ultor' becomes 'vindex et ultor', as in the Ambrosianus. The note that Lysias' name was banned from wedding rites is omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,23 (Müller XXIII) = Kübler cap. 16, pp. 26–27 (Jakobi 1,23,658)
parallels.change: The Methone episode is compressed. The envoys become 'Darii regis Persarum legatio' demanding tribute, 'earth and water'. Alexander's message changes: in Valerius he threatens to reclaim the tribute and seize Persia's own wealth; in Z he says the king will otherwise face him in battle. 'Ne litterarum quidem … dignatus' and Philip's pride in his son are omitted. 'Deficeret' is a reading shared by Z and the Ambrosianus.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,24 (Müller XXIV) = Kübler cap. 17–18, pp. 27–28 (Jakobi 1,24,690, 718)
parallels.change:
Pausanias' Thessalonican origin is omitted.
'Ecquid mulier consentiret … neque id ei ex sententia provenisset' becomes 'et mulier consentiret', with the failure clause missing, so Olympias seems to consent. In the Greek and in Valerius she refuses. This is a ZA conjunctive error noted by Calderan, Rosellini and Jakobi.
The theatre games are not introduced, though 'in theatro' remains.
Ammon is removed twice: Olympias' 'habeo praesidem Ammonem' is omitted, and Philip's 'ab Ammone dicta' becomes 'deum … praedixisse'.
The mourning of Macedonia and Greece is omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,25 (Müller XXV) = Kübler cap. 19–20, pp. 28–30 (Jakobi 1,25,725)
parallels.change: The speech loses its address to Pella, Athens and Corinth and the call to 'enslave the Persians'; the edict to the cities is omitted. 'Ac si divinitus monitus' is kept. The veterans' refusal and Alexander's speech on youth and age (Kübler cap. 20) are skipped. Z preserves 'en' with T against AP (Jakobi).

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,26 (Müller XXVI) = Kübler cap. 21, pp. 30–31 (Siemoneit 1,26,770–773)
parallels.change: The troop figures are kept, with a total of 70,604 (as in T; Kübler prints 70,654). The second source of funds and the sums in talents become 'abundantissime'. The warships and transports and Thrace's inherited loyalty are omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,29 (Müller XXIX) = Kübler cap. 22, p. 31
parallels.ps_call_alpha: Ps.-Call. α 1.29 (α has no 1.27–28; per Kroll these are β-only)
parallels.change: The Thracian levies and 400 talents are omitted. 'Communi sacrificio foederatis' becomes 'ad amicitiam foederatis', dropping the sacrifice. The Sicilian subjugation clause is cut, as is the crown's weight (100 lb), which Z simply calls 'aurea'. Rome's gift of 'talenta quadringenta' becomes 'quadraginta' (400 → 40). Rome's war with Carthage is omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,30 (Müller XXX) = Kübler cap. 22 end–23, pp. 31–33 (Siemoneit 1,30,800–814)
Iul. Val. 1,34 (Müller XXXIV) = Kübler cap. 33–34, pp. 43–45
parallels.change: The opening sentence is kept almost verbatim. Omitted: the hard march; the Egyptians coming out with images of their gods; Memphis and the temple of Hephaestus. 'Iuniorem Sesonchosim' becomes 'secundum Sesonchosin'. The enthronement clause ('veste et sede regni dignum duxerunt') equals a marginal reading in the Ambrosianus; that manuscript's second hand drew variants from Z. The statue's prophetic inscription is omitted, as are Alexander's speech on Egypt's walls and wealth and his demand for Darius' tribute (Kübler cap. 34).

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,35 (Müller XXXV) = Kübler cap. 35–36, pp. 45–47
Iul. Val. 1,36 (Müller XXXVI) = Kübler cap. 37, pp. 47–48 (Siemoneit; Jakobi 1,36,1205–1215)
parallels.change: Darius' title loses 'consessorque dei Mithrae … oriens cum sole'. 'Latrocinantium ritu' becomes 'ritu latronum', and 'quod subfecerit' becomes 'quo tibi tuisque necessaria emas'. The ending is expanded into 'qui te vinctum atque contumeliose verberibus affectum … deducant'; Kinzel notes that Lamprecht v. 1486 agrees with this Epitome wording.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,37 (Müller XXXVII) = Kübler cap. 38–39, pp. 48–50
parallels.change: The 'barking dogs' speech is kept nearly verbatim, without its final sentences. Added: 'Atque his dictis roborat pavitantia corda suorum'. Omitted: the order to crucify the envoys, their plea, Alexander's relenting, the banquet, and the envoy's offer to betray Darius, which Alexander declines. The return of the gold is kept.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,38 (Müller XXXVIII) = Kübler cap. 40, pp. 50–51
parallels.change: The salutation drops the parents and 'consessori dei Mithrae … orienti, maximo Persarum domino' and keeps 'consanguineo deorum'. Omitted: the remarks on divine titles, 'adero ut mortalis', and the two possible outcomes (Persian empire or 'robbery suppressed'). The reading of the strap, ball and gold is kept, but the gold as 'annual price of servitude' is dropped.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,39 (Müller XXXIX) = Kübler cap. 41–42, pp. 51–52
parallels.change: Alexander's conquest of Syria is cut. Darius' order to the satraps is turned from reported speech into direct speech, without the knucklebones and rattles, the Persian tutor and the distribution of horses. In the satraps' reply their names (Hystaspes and Spinther), 'deo Dario' and the five captives are omitted. Darius' angry reply to the satraps (Kübler cap. 42) is omitted.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,40 (Müller XL) = Kübler cap. 42 end, pp. 52–53 (Jakobi 1,40,1347)
parallels.change: The setting (Alexander camped by a river) and Darius' 'lord of 120 nations' are omitted. The letter is abridged: the crossing of the sea, the 'Graeculi' and the threat of punishment are gone. The oath by Jupiter and his ancestors is kept. Z has 'ad' with Rosellini against AP.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,41 (Müller XLI) = Kübler cap. 43–44, pp. 53–56 (Siemoneit: lines 1361–1373)
parallels.change: The battle is told rather than shown. Omitted: the wings, Amyntas son of Antiochus, Darius hiding his chariot, the 60 stades, Alexander in the Persian tents, the praise of his moderation, and the figures for casualties and booty. Added: Darius becomes 'praecursor' of the flight (D and E read 'praecessor'). The burial of the fallen and the courteous treatment of Darius' family are kept.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,42 (Müller XLII) = Kübler cap. 45–47, pp. 56–59
Iul. Val. 1,46 (Müller XLVI) = Kübler cap. 51–53, pp. 61–64 (Siemoneit 1,46,1556–1560; Jakobi 1,46,1568)
parallels.ps_call_alpha: Ps.-Call. α 1.46 and 1.46a (Ismenias) (Kroll pp. 52–61, markers checked)
parallels.change: Alexander's demand for 1,000 Thebans and their refusal are omitted, so the attack is less motivated (Siemoneit). Valerius' ironic 'o vos fortissimos' becomes 'o vos stultissimos … dicam', which matches a marginal 'vel stultissimos dixerim' in the Ambrosianus. 'Iaculisque ac telis debellare' is in Z but not in AP; Jakobi argues it is genuine Valerius (cf. the Greek), not an addition. Omitted: the walls built by lyre music, the fire and rams, and the slingers. The piper's plea is cut to Liber, Hercules, Amphion and Zethus, without the orgia, Semele and Alcmena; he is not named, here or in Valerius. Alexander is called 'tyranni', and his retort is turned into narrative.

parallels.jv: Iul. Val. 1,47 (Müller XLVII; begins at 'Sed Thebani, quicumque fugae…') = Kübler cap. 53 end–54, pp. 64–65
parallels.ps_call_alpha: Ps.-Call. α 1.47 (Kroll pp. 61–63; marker at the Clitomachus episode checked); the oracle stands at the 1.46a/1.47 junction
parallels.change: The two-line Delphic oracle is kept verbatim, and Clitomachus' triple victory and speech follow Valerius closely. 'Certamen gymnicum' becomes 'sollemne certamen', and 'condi Thebas' becomes 'reaedificari Thebas'. The order of the gods changes to Hercules, Mercury, Pollux (Valerius: Mercury, Hercules, Pollux).

= North Africa.

Ammon's herald (chs. 6–7, 10); the omen of the egg (ch. 11).
Sacred bird sent to Philip.
Grows 'only in our land', i.e. Egypt.
A rare word, also in Valerius.

Nurse. The Greek tradition has Lanike (Λανίκη), sister of Cleitus the Black (Kroll's apparatus).

Music teacher; 'Lemnius' in Valerius, dropped in Z.

intro_ru:
«Эпитома Юлия Валерия» («эпитома Цахера»)

Перед вами анонимное латинское сокращение «Деяний Александра Македонского» (Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis) Юлия Валерия Александра Полемия. Это латинский перевод греческого «Романа об Александре» Псевдо-Каллисфена (древнейшая редакция α), выполненный в начале IV в. Сокращение принято называть «эпитомой Цахера» по имени первого и пока единственного издателя, германиста Юлиуса Цахера (Галле, 1867).

Время и место создания эпитомы неизвестны. Древнейшие рукописи относятся к началу IX в.: Гаага, Королевская библиотека, 74 J 9, и Лейден, Voss. lat. Q 20. Поэтому привычная датировка VIII–IX вв. даёт лишь верхнюю границу (terminus ante quem), и текст может быть старше. Предположение о его италийском происхождении оспаривается.

Значение памятника определила его судьба. Полный Юлий Валерий дошёл в немногих неполных свидетелях, а эпитома — примерно в восьмидесяти рукописях; она фактически вытеснила оригинал. Для начальных глав романа она, вместе со своей расширенной оксфордской переработкой, остаётся единственным источником латинского текста. Через эпитому сюжет вошёл в «Историческое зерцало» Винсента из Бове и в хронику Элинана из Фруамона. К ней или к полному Юлию Валерию восходит «Александр» Альберика из Писансона, а через него — немецкая «Песнь об Александре» Лампрехта. По мнению ряда исследователей, эпитомой пользовался и Томас Кентский.

Эпитоматор сократил текст примерно до трети, причём первая книга сохранена полнее остальных. Он держится слов Юлия Валерия, но упрощает лексику и синтаксис. Он опускает подробности сражений, языческие обряды и оракулы, большую часть упоминаний Аммона и всё, что бросает тень на Александра. По выражению Г. Зимонайта, получилась «безобидная редакция» романа. Иногда сокращение меняет смысл. Оскорбительная шутка Лисия на свадьбе Филиппа заменена нейтральной фразой. В рассказе о Павсании Олимпиада, отвергшая его у Юлия Валерия, вдруг оказывается «согласной» — это порча, общая с одной из рукописей полного Валерия.

Первая книга охватывает «рождение» Александра в широком смысле:
- египетская магия Нектанеба и его бегство в Македонию;
- обольщение Олимпиады под видом бога Аммона, знамения и рождение Александра;
- его воспитание, гибель Нектанеба от руки сына, укрощение Буцефала, состязание в Олимпии;
- разлад и примирение родителей, убийство Филиппа Павсанием и воцарение Александра;
- поход в Италию, Ливию и Египет, взятие Тира, обмен посланиями с Дарием и первая победа над ним.
Завершается книга разрушением Фив и сценой с кулачным бойцом Клитомахом в Коринфе.

Перевод выполнен по изданию Цахера в TEI-транскрипции Г. Зимонайта (лицензия CC0). Нумерация глав принадлежит Цахеру: он разметил текст по главам издания К. Мюллера (1846), общим для Псевдо-Каллисфена и Юлия Валерия. Поэтому номера идут с пропусками (нет глав 16, 27–28, 31–33, 43–45): это главы, которых в эпитоме нет; глав 27–28 нет и у Юлия Валерия. Зато номер главы сразу указывает на соответствующее место Юлия Валерия в издании М. Розеллини и греческой редакции α в издании В. Кролля. Эти параллели отмечены на полях.

Необходимы оговорки. Современного критического издания эпитомы нет. Цахер использовал лишь семь из примерно восьмидесяти рукописей, хотя и древнейшие, готовил книгу в спешке и почти не вносил исправлений. Расширенные версии эпитомы (оксфордская и монпельевская) и лигницкая переработка здесь не учитываются. Насколько нам удалось установить, на современные языки эпитома прежде не переводилась. Черновик перевода подготовлен с помощью ИИ и проходит проверку редактора.

— Редакция Neoscholia
